title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
section: The Democratic caucus is favoured to control the Senate, 52 seats to 48
text:
The Democratic caucus is favoured to control the Senate, 52 seats to 48
We combine synthetic responses from four language models with polling information to forecast the 35 Senate races in 2026. To estimate which party will control the Senate, we add the 35 race predictions to the 65 seats not up for election: 31 held by Republicans, 32 by Democrats, and two by independents, Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats.
The probability that the Democratic caucus reaches the 51-seat threshold for control, without support from newly elected independents, is 61 per cent; the probability that Republicans retain control is 37 per cent. Republicans need 50 seats because the Republican vice president can break a 50–50 tie. The remaining simulations require a decision about newly elected independents, whose caucus affiliations we do not assume. In 90 per cent of our simulations, Republicans win between 40 and 55 seats, showing the uncertainty around the forecast.



This summary shows all 100 Senate seats, with each model weighted equally. The Democratic caucus includes Sanders and King; any independent seats shown represent newly elected independents. Republican and newly elected independent seat counts are medians, with the remaining seats assigned to the Democratic caucus.



Democrats are favoured to gain North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, now held by Republicans. Maine, Iowa and Texas are toss-ups, with each side given a winning probability of 45% to 55%.

title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
text:
How the forecast works
We forecast all 35 Senate races on 3 November 2026 by combining synthetic voter responses with polling information. We sample 100 personas per state from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Each persona receives nine news paragraphs, and four language models answer its voting question three times in their own words. We score these answers using Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR), then average the scores to estimate each state’s Republican share of the two-candidate vote.
The models’ synthetic Republican vote shares are, on average, 5–9 percentage points higher than the polling estimates. We subtract each model’s average difference from the polls to correct for this bias. This correction is based on polling estimates rather than actual election results. We then combine the adjusted model estimate with the state’s polling average. For states without polling data, we instead use the 2024 CES vote share, adjusted by the average shift observed in states with polls. When combining the two estimates, we give less weight to the estimate with greater uncertainty, following the approach of Lock and Gelman (2010), but our error estimates are approximate. We simulate 1,000 election outcomes for each model, allowing a shared national error to affect multiple states at the same time. We give all four models equal weight and include the 65 Senate seats that are not up for election to estimate each party’s probability of controlling the Senate. In the Discussion, we compare this combined forecast with three alternative forecasting methods.

title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
text:
Methods
The voting responses are synthetic; we did not conduct a new survey. We used Python 3.12 (Python Software Foundation 2023) with pandas (McKinney 2010), NumPy (Harris et al. 2020), pyarrow (Apache Arrow Developers 2026), matplotlib (Hunter 2007), requests (Reitz 2026), lxml (Behnel et al. 2026), tqdm (da Costa-Luis 2019) and python-dotenv (Kumar 2026). Pilot embeddings used sentence-transformers (Reimers and Gurevych 2019). Tests use pytest (Krekel et al. 2004) and pandera (Bantilan 2020), and the website was built with Quarto (Allaire et al. 2026).

Data
Our personas come from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES), a survey of 60,000 US adults (Schaffner et al. 2025; Ansolabehere et al. 2025). Of these respondents, 38,307 lived in the 35 states holding Senate elections in 2026. Among them, 23,025 had a post-election voter-file weight, and 21,211 were validated as having voted in 2024. We chose the post-election weight because the persona characteristics use both survey waves. A voter-file weight does not by itself show that a respondent voted, so we applied the validated-voter restriction separately.
We obtained candidate lists from Wikipedia on 21 October (Wikipedia contributors 2026). Each race pairs the Republican with the leading Democratic or Independent opponent. Where several names were listed for a side, we selected the candidate appearing most often in polls since 1 August. The opponents in Idaho, Nebraska and South Dakota are Independent. In Montana, Independent Seth Bodnar polls ahead of Democrat Alani Bankhead. The prompts acknowledge additional candidates without naming them individually.
We corrected Montana’s candidate pair before the 31 October run. The 27 and 29 October runs paired Republican Kurt Alme with Bankhead rather than Bodnar. Their synthetic estimates and matched polls therefore described a different contest, so those Montana results are not directly comparable with the final run.
Polling data come from PollResults, which compiles Senate polls originally tracked by The New York Times (PollResults.org 2026). We use them in the combined forecast and as a benchmark for the synthetic estimates. Polls estimate voter preferences; they are not election results. Their role in setting the weights is described below.


Personas
Each persona describes a respondent’s age, education, race, gender, household income, ideology and party identification. Age is measured in 2024 and grouped as 18–29, 30–44, 45–64 or 65+. Education ranges from less than high school to a postgraduate degree. Race has five categories: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian and Other. Gender distinguishes men, women, non-binary respondents and other responses. Income retains the survey’s 16 brackets and its “Prefer not to say” option. Ideology ranges from very liberal to very conservative, while party identification distinguishes strong, weak and leaning partisans from Independents. Uncertain responses are retained as “Not sure.” The models do not see the respondent’s reported 2024 presidential vote, which we reserve for descriptive comparisons.


Weighted sampling
We draw 100 personas in each state, with replacement, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Using replacement in every state keeps the procedure consistent, including in Wyoming and Alaska, whose eligible pools contain only 52 and 76 respondents. Across the sample, 904 of the 3,500 personas repeat someone already selected in the same state. About two-thirds of the selections in Alaska and Wyoming are repeats, so 100 personas do not mean 100 distinct people.
Survey weights determine which respondents are drawn; they are not applied again when answers are aggregated. Wang et al. (2015), by contrast, adjusted an opt-in Xbox sample after collecting responses, using multilevel regression and post-stratification. Our weighted draw reproduces each state’s weighted CES composition in expectation, and each selected persona counts equally within its state. Applying the survey weights again would double-weight the sample. The procedure does not account for changes in the electorate between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms. Equal state sample sizes support separate race forecasts, but pooled demographic comparisons require state-level weighting, as explained in Crosstabs.


News summaries
We collect news from publisher RSS feeds, with Google News site searches as a fallback. Each collection covers the preceding 48 hours, removes duplicates and keeps up to 60 items per outlet. The collected titles, feed excerpts and URLs are saved in the repository (data/01-raw_data/news/). The ten outlets are The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Fox News, New York Post, The Daily Wire, HuffPost, Mother Jones and Vox. We group them as left-leaning outlets, newspapers and right-leaning outlets, following Pew Research Center’s audience and political-leaning information (Shearer et al. 2025). “Newspapers” identifies a source group, not political neutrality.
GPT-4.1 Nano (OpenAI 2025) screens titles and feed excerpts for US national significance and relevance to elections, policy, law or the economy. It then writes a short paragraph for each retained item. The instructions exclude sports and unrelated material and require a concrete development. Selected incorrect presidential and vice-presidential titles trigger a rewrite or exclusion. The paragraphs rely on titles and excerpts, not full articles, and the checks do not independently verify their claims.
Each persona receives nine paragraphs, with three drawn at random from each source group. We concatenate the existing paragraphs without another model summary. The same news block is used across models and repeat queries. A fixed random seed reproduces the selection when inputs are unchanged, and retries reuse the dated selections. Example: the news block of one persona (Florida, 31 October)

Each of the 3,500 personas received nine paragraphs, three from each source group, drawn at random from that day’s kept articles (published 30 October 10:00 to 31 October 21:27 UTC). For illustration, we selected the archived block for persona FL_12, reproduced word for word. This example was not randomly selected and does not establish the quality of all news blocks.

Vox reports: Republicans are facing criticism for their vote to shrink Medicaid by roughly $1 trillion over the next decade, a move that is expected to leave more than 7 million Americans without healthcare coverage, impacting voter opinions in the 2026 midterm elections.
The New York Times reports: An article suggests that the upcoming election may bring significant political changes, regardless of the outcome of a Democratic sweep or not.
The Washington Post reports: A longtime Texas Republican reportedly split his ticket due to rising costs, reflecting economic concerns influencing voter and politician behavior.
The New York Times reports: Obamacare policies are experiencing steep premium increases for 2027, affecting nationwide healthcare affordability and policy discussions.
Fox News reports: A South Korean government-commissioned study suggests paper straws may pose health risks, scoring significantly higher than plastic on a cancer-related measure, raising questions about their environmental and health impacts.
Fox News reports: Mark Levin claims there was a conspiracy to steal the Senate, reflecting ongoing political debates and allegations concerning election integrity.
New York Post reports: The article discusses the possibility of military strikes against Iran by Israel, which could impact US foreign policy and security considerations.
Vox reports: A great deal is at stake in next week’s midterm elections. The partisan makeup of the new Congress will shape future spending bills, investigations, and judicial nominations, affecting US policy and governance.
HuffPost reports: JD Vance’s response to a young voter’s question about affordability has been criticized by experts, highlighting ongoing debates over economic policy.




Prompts and models
We ask each persona how it would vote in its state’s Senate race and randomise the order of the two candidates. Models from four companies allow for systematic differences in their responses (Murray and Alexander 2026). We record the returned model identifier and query time because a model can change while retaining its advertised name (Bisbee et al. 2024).
We use Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic 2026), GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI 2026), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek 2026) and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (Google 2026a) through OpenRouter (OpenRouter 2026). Each model answers every persona’s prompt three times. We score the responses separately and average their scores to reduce variation between individual answers. We request two or three sentences rather than percentages, leave generation temperature at the provider’s default, and cap output at 800 tokens. Reasoning is disabled except for Gemini, which requires it and uses minimal effort. Empty, refused and otherwise invalid responses are recorded and excluded from scoring, rather than assigned zero support. Four Claude Haiku calls returned no answer in the 31 October run; calls and answers by model appear in the cost table.


Turning answers into voting probabilities

Why free-text answers?
LLM responses can concentrate on a small set of answers, a problem known as mode collapse. Heath and Alexander (2026) study whether free-text responses scored with Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR) better reproduce distributions in rating tasks. Maier et al. (2025) introduced SSR for purchase-intent ratings. We use this free-text approach for voting questions, without assuming that it prevents mode collapse.


Choosing the embedding model
On 26 October, we compared embedding models on 200 generated answers from Florida personas without news, 50 per voting model. Keyword rules identified 159 answers with a clear candidate choice. MiniLM placed 12 on the opposite side of the two-candidate scale; Gemini Embedding 2 misplaced one. MiniLM’s errors involved answers supporting Nixon that also mentioned Moody. Adding both names to each anchor worsened performance, so we retained single-candidate anchors and selected Gemini Embedding 2.
This diagnostic does not validate scoring across all states. Neither setup captured indecision well: answers expressing it received an average weight of 0.14 on the middle category. Leaning and definite statements also often received similar scores. These findings informed the embedder choice while showing the limits of interpreting SSR weights as voting probabilities.


Semantic Similarity Rating
Gemini Embedding 2 (Google 2026b) represents each answer and five candidate-specific statements as numerical vectors. The statements express definite support for the Democratic or Independent candidate, leaning toward that candidate, being undecided or choosing another option, leaning Republican, and definite Republican support. Cosine similarity compares the direction of the answer’s vector with each statement’s vector, producing five similarity scores per answer.
We rescale those five scores to the range zero to one and apply softmax with a temperature of 0.25. Adding the first two weights gives support for the Democratic or Independent candidate; adding the final two gives Republican support. The middle weight represents other choices, indecision or nonvoting. Answers and statements are embedded in the same way, without separate query and document settings.
These allocations are not calibrated probabilities of an individual’s actual vote. Vote choice is not an ordered rating scale, and the middle statement groups behaviours with different meanings. We neither apply a smoothing step nor fit the temperature to voting outcomes, which are not yet observed. This differs from the rating applications in Heath and Alexander (2026). Softmax may assign weight to both sides even when an answer clearly names one candidate. That allocation reflects the scoring rule, not greater variation between personas.



Combining synthetic votes with polls
We draw on Lock and Gelman’s (2010) inverse-variance approach to combining forecasts and polls. They estimate predictive uncertainty from past elections. We adapt the weighting idea using approximate error scales for synthetic responses, rather than reproducing their full Bayesian model.
We first average each persona’s scores over repeated answers. The state’s Republican two-candidate share is the mean Republican score divided by the sum of the mean scores for the two candidates. Resampling personas 1,000 times estimates its bootstrap variability. The outside estimate uses information other than synthetic responses: a state polling average where available, or the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”) otherwise. Polls must name both selected candidates and end within 45 days of the newest poll. We retain one question per poll, prefer likely-voter samples and weight two-candidate shares by sample size.
The combination has two steps. First, we subtract each model’s average synthetic–poll gap across polled states to obtain the corrected share \(m^*\). This assumes that polls are correct on average across those states; it does not establish that the original gap was a model error. Second, we combine \(m^*\) with the outside estimate \(t\): \(c=(1-w)m^*+wt\), with outside weight \(w=V_m/(V_m+V_t)\). A larger synthetic variance gives the outside estimate more weight. The synthetic variance \(V_m\) adds bootstrap variance to a structural variance. We estimate the structural component from the across-state variance of the differences between corrected synthetic shares and polling averages, subtracting the average bootstrap and polling variances. A floor of \(0.005^2\) keeps this component positive.
For polls, the error scale adds sampling variance \(p(1-p)/n\) to an assumed \(0.03^2\) for error beyond sampling (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018). For states without polls, it uses the errors around 2024 plus uniform swing. We draw normal outcomes around the combined share with variance \(1/(1/V_m+1/V_t)\), then add a shared national error with standard deviation 0.03. The correction applies each model’s average synthetic–poll gap equally to every state. The weights also assume that synthetic and polling errors are independent. These assumptions make the estimates approximate. The Discussion compares the combined forecast with synthetic-only and no-LLM forecasts, and with a version that retains the gap and counts it as error.


Sources of uncertainty
The simulations account for persona resampling, estimated structural synthetic error after correction, uncertainty in polls or the historical benchmark, and a national error shared across states. Pooling the four models retains their disagreements. However, the average gap, variances and swing are estimated from the same polled states and treated as fixed. We do not separately model regional errors or dependence between synthetic and polling errors. The sensitivity analysis varies the assumed national and polling errors to show their effect on Senate control.


Tests
Before the full runs, we tested the workflow with five personas per state, free Laguna and Nemotron models, and a local MiniLM embedder. Separate pytest and pandera suites check the simulated data and actual runs. They test individual tables and consistency across the sample, answers, scores and forecasts.
The tests account for expected model–persona combinations and repeats, recorded failures, the returned provider and token usage. Missing or refused answers must remain missing after scoring. Valid scores must lie between zero and one and sum to one. Forecasts must assign valid vote shares and winners, fill all 100 Senate seats and keep the weighted estimate between its two inputs. Another check verifies that the combination uses the saved synthetic estimate and recorded weights.
We checked the tests by introducing missing probabilities, probabilities summing to 1.3, invalid vote-share totals and answers from another provider into a copy of earlier data. Each error was caught. Failed tests stop publication while preserving paid answers. Passing these checks supports consistency of the calculations, not election accuracy.


Design
We used election coverage from CNN, Politico, NPR, CBC and Reuters as design references (CNN 2024; Politico 2024; NPR 2024; CBC News 2024; Reuters 2024). The website and figures share a colour palette, typography and table style so readers can compare results without relearning the presentation.

Evaluation
The forecast cannot be scored against the actual results until after the election on 3 November. Therefore, we compare it with a prediction market that forecasts the same races using a different method.

Against a prediction market
This comparison follows Wang et al. (2015), who compared their Xbox-based election forecasts with prediction markets before election results were available. We use PredictIt (PredictIt 2026), which has a market for each of the 35 races and for control of the Senate. It provides another forecast to compare with, rather than ground truth, and combines information through trading (Rothschild 2009).
For each news day, we use the daily closing prices returned by PredictIt’s API, rather than a live quote. A winning contract pays one dollar, so its price roughly reflects a probability. We normalise the two selected contract prices so that they sum to one: the Republican probability is its closing price divided by the sum of both prices. Third candidates are excluded to match our two-candidate framework. title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
text:
Discussion

Comparing four ways of building the forecast
The table compares four methods using the latest run’s saved inputs. Synthetic-only uses the original SSR shares without polling adjustment. The combined forecast, used for the headline, subtracts each model’s average gap from polls and combines the corrected shares with state polling averages. Where polls are unavailable, it uses the 2024 CES vote share shifted by the average change in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”). The third version combines raw synthetic shares with the outside estimates. Its error scale uses the mean squared synthetic–poll gap instead of the variance of the remaining differences after correction. Both the input shares and weights therefore change. The no-LLM benchmark uses the same polling averages and 2024-plus-swing estimates, excluding synthetic responses. The comparison shows how synthetic responses change the forecast, but cannot establish accuracy before election results are available.

The synthetic methods pool four models with equal weight. Seat intervals contain the middle 90% of simulated outcomes.

For 31 October, adding polling and historical information lowers the Republican control probability from 90% in the synthetic-only forecast to 37%. The no-LLM benchmark gives 34%; including synthetic responses moves the combined forecast toward greater Republican support. Synthetic estimates receive an average weight of 19% in polled states and 17% in unpolled states. The remaining weight goes to state polling averages or, where unavailable, the 2024 CES vote share plus uniform swing. These outside estimates therefore dominate the combined result. In the comparison without bias correction, we combine the original synthetic shares with polling and historical estimates. Including the synthetic–poll gap in the error estimate gives synthetic shares an average weight of 11% in polled states. This version gives Republicans a 42% probability of control, compared with 37% under the bias-corrected headline forecast. The versions differ in both their synthetic shares and weights.


Do synthetic voters reproduce partisan voting patterns?
Argyle et al. (2023) define algorithmic fidelity as a model’s ability to reproduce patterns of human responses across groups. We compare synthetic Republican support in the 2026 Senate races with the same personas’ reported Republican vote in the 2024 presidential election, across demographic and party-identification groups. The prompts did not include that earlier vote. The comparison asks whether the models reproduce earlier partisan patterns, not whether they predict each person’s next vote. Because some Senate opponents are Independents, non-Republican support cannot always be labelled Democratic support. In the 31 October run, 54 per cent of all personas leaned Republican, against a 55 per cent Republican vote in 2024, and every gender, race, age, education and income group with at least 50 personas was within 6 points, except personas without a high-school diploma (54 against 63 per cent).
Bisbee et al. (2024) caution that aggregate resemblance can mask overly uniform responses and distorted relationships between characteristics and opinions. The Crosstabs table compares synthetic Republican support with reported 2024 Republican voting across these groups. Party-identification groups help assess whether the models rely too heavily on party. Weak Republicans leaned Republican 97 per cent of the time, against a 92 per cent Republican vote in 2024; weak Democrats leaned Republican 5 against 13 per cent. Groups without a clear party preference offer a harder check: Independents leaned Republican 41 per cent of the time, against 61 per cent in 2024. Agreement with the 2024 column is not enough: turnout, candidates and preferences can change between elections. In the polled states, the polls put the Democratic side about 6 points above its 2024 share, while the synthetic shares sit 5 to 9 points on the Republican side of the polls. We use the tables to describe the synthetic sample, not to validate the forecast.


Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating
SSR scores do not always match the strength of support expressed in an answer (Heath and Alexander 2026; Maier et al. 2025). The scoring rule can assign support to both candidates even when a response clearly chooses one: strong Democrats leaned Republican in 1 per cent of cases, but their average Republican SSR share was 14 per cent. A group can therefore appear less partisan without its personas’ answers becoming more diverse. Our limited embedding check also found that undecided answers were not clearly distinguished from candidate support. The forecast depends partly on the reference statements and softmax temperature, as well as on the model answers.


The news the personas read
Murray and Alexander (2026) find that including party identification in a persona can limit the effect of news on its answers. Our news comparison shows small changes in the average synthetic share across the recorded runs, with different changes across states. Every prompt includes party identification, which may contribute to this stability. Model answers also vary between runs, so we cannot attribute all changes to news exposure or infer that news has no effect on real voters.


Uncertainty and the correlation between states
The sensitivity table shows how error assumptions affect the probability of Senate control. If polls miss support for one party across the country, several closely matched races could change winners together (Gelman et al. 2020). Errors confined to one region may produce patterns that our shared national error does not fully capture. The forecasts change little across the three days, but their wide seat intervals allow many outcomes. Stability alone does not establish accuracy.


What agreement with the market tells us
Our forecast and PredictIt agree across many states in the market comparison. Much of the high correlation may come from races with a strongly favoured candidate. Disagreements in closely matched races matter more when a few seats could change Senate control. Traders can read the polls used in our combined forecast, so agreement is not an independent check of polling information. Low trading activity and how traders value unlikely outcomes can also affect prices (Rothschild 2009; Wang et al. 2015). The comparison provides context; election results are needed to assess accuracy.


Limitations
We lack results from past elections with which to estimate this synthetic method’s typical forecast error. Unlike Lock and Gelman (2010), we therefore use approximate error estimates rather than historical forecast performance. Polls provide a benchmark, but can miss nonrespondents, misjudge turnout or become outdated as preferences change. Subtracting each model’s average synthetic–poll gap can carry a shared polling error into the corrected synthetic estimates. The comparison without bias correction retains the gap and gives synthetic estimates less weight. The method comparison shows that both the input shares and weighting rules affect the result; neither version is known to be more accurate.
The uncertainty estimates rely on assumptions. As described in Sources of uncertainty, estimated error sizes are fixed and not all dependencies are modelled, which may make seat intervals too narrow. The additional polling error has an assumed standard deviation of 3 percentage points, not a value established for these races; the sensitivity table also considers 2 and 4 points. Polls from one aggregator may still share errors (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018). The bootstrap also treats repeated selections of a CES respondent as separate personas. This may understate uncertainty, especially in Alaska and Wyoming, where respondent pools are small.
In the 10 states without usable polls, the outside estimate is the 2024 CES vote share plus uniform swing. A common shift does not account for the appeal of individual Senate candidates. Synthetic estimates may also misrepresent the relationship between demographic characteristics, party identification and candidate choice. In Kentucky, for example, many personas identify as Democrats but describe themselves as conservative. Their synthetic support should not be assumed to measure actual support for the Senate candidates.
The forecast considers only two candidates per race, so the final two-candidate shares do not fully represent other candidates, indecision or nonvoting. In Montana, we compare Republican Kurt Alme with Independent Seth Bodnar and omit Democrat Alani Bankhead. The forecast cannot represent support across all three candidates or how that division affects the winner. Further scoring limitations are discussed under Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating.
Provider defaults and model updates can change answers even when prompts are saved. News was collected on only three days, limiting what these runs tell us about responses to other events. Future work could vary the amount and mix of news while holding the remaining inputs constant.
Comparable forecasts from more elections would allow us to test the correction and weights. They could also help assess whether error sizes differ by region or race competitiveness, whether models should receive different weights, and whether estimating uncertainty across dates gives more reliable results.


Conclusion: what the synthetic voters add
Synthetic-only strongly favours Republican control, while the combined forecast and no-LLM benchmark favour the Democratic caucus. Synthetic responses change the result relative to the no-LLM benchmark, but receive a small share of the combined weight. The project illustrates how silicon sampling can enter an election forecast; it does not establish an improvement over polling and historical information. Evaluation against election results must use the same vote-share denominator: votes for the two selected candidates, not all candidates. Winner comparisons must also account for omitted candidates who could win or affect the outcome, especially in Montana. Assessing the method more broadly requires more elections and settings.
